sections.content: Automated verification instead of human preferences. For math: calculator. For code: unit tests. {term:reward:Reward} is binary: RIGHT (1.0) or WRONG (0.0). No humans, scales infinitely.
Binary {term:reward:reward} from deterministic verifiers. No neural {term:reward:reward} {term:model:model}.

sections.title: Verification
sections.content:
Math: "847 × 23 = 19481" → calculator → TRUE → R=1.0
Code: is_prime → run_tests → pass → R=1.0
Limit: Only verifiable tasks

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content:
What it measures: The gap between 'how much my model prefers the winner' vs 'how much my model prefers the loser'.

• Positive margin → Model correctly prefers winner
• Negative margin → Model wrongly prefers loser
• Larger positive → More confident and correct

sections.title: Intuitive Definition
sections.content:
What it does: Controls how much we update on each example.

• Model is correct (winner > loser) → weight is SMALL → small update
• Model is wrong (loser > winner) → weight is LARGE → strong update

Why it matters: Focuses learning on mistakes. Prevents over-optimizing already-solved examples, which would cause mode collapse.

content.title: The Mechanical Difference
content.content:
{term:sft:SFT} (Imitation): Minimizes prediction {term:loss:loss} against fixed human examples. The {term:gradient:gradient} points toward "what the human wrote".

RL (Optimization): Maximizes a {term:reward:reward} signal. The {term:gradient:gradient} points toward "whatever gave a high score".

content.title: How {term:sft:SFT} Creates the "Average"
content.content:
The Scenario: You have 5 examples of "How to greet".
• 2 examples say "Hi!"
• 2 examples say "Hello there."
• 1 example says "Greetings."

The Mechanics:
• {term:model:Model} predicts "Hi": {term:loss:Loss} = 0 for some, High for others.
• {term:gradient:Gradient} descent minimizes TOTAL {term:loss:loss}.
• Optimum: The {term:model:model} learns to output a probability distribution that mixes them: 40% Hi, 40% Hello, 20% Greetings.

The Trap: It becomes a "probabilistic average" of the training data. It cannot be BETTER than the data.

content.title: How RL Finds the "Peak"
content.content:
The Scenario: Same greeting task, but we score them.
• "Hi!" → {term:reward:R} = 0.5
• "Hello there." → {term:reward:R} = 0.6
• "Greetings." → {term:reward:R} = 0.9 (User loves this one!)

The Mechanics:
• RL objective: Maximize Expected {term:reward:Reward}.
• {term:policy:Policy} Update: Shift probability mass from low reward to high reward.
• {term:gradient:Gradient} pushes P("Greetings") → 1.0.

Result: The {term:model:model} IGNORES the "average" (Hi/Hello) and collapses onto the "peak" strategy (Greetings). It surpasses the majority of its training data!
SFT Mechanics: For the full math of Next-Token Prediction and Loss, see our Training & Fine-Tuning topic.

slides.title: What Does RL Actually Do? (The Scoring Coach)

content.title: The Key Difference
content.content:
{term:sft:SFT}: "Here's a perfect response. Copy it exactly."
RL: "Generate whatever you want. I'll tell you how good it was. Do better next time."

{term:sft:SFT} = learning from textbook.
RL = learning from coach who grades performance.

content.title: RL Training Loop
content.content:
There IS no fixed dataset. The {term:model:model} generates its own training {term:data:data}!

1. Prompt: "Explain quantum physics simply"
2. {term:model:Model} generates multiple responses
   • A: "Particles can be waves..." → {term:reward:R} = 0.73
   • B: "Imagine tiny balls..." → {term:reward:R} = 0.89 ← Best!
   • C: "Quantum mechanics states..." → {term:reward:R} = 0.62
3. Update: Make {term:model:model} more likely to generate B-like responses

The {term:model:model} explores and learns which STRATEGIES work.

content.title: Step-by-Step RL Training
content.content:
Step 1 - Generate:
• Prompt: "What is 12 × 15?" → Response: "Let me calculate: 180"

Step 2 - Score:
• {term:rlhf:RLHF}: Neural {term:reward:reward} {term:model:model} → {term:reward:R} = 0.78
• {term:rlvr:RLVR}: Rule verifier → {term:reward:R} = 1.0 (correct!)

Step 3 - Advantage:
• Was this better than expected? {term:advantage:A} = 0.78 - 0.65 = +0.13

Step 4 - Update:
• Increase {term:probability:P} of {term:token:tokens} that led to high {term:reward:reward}
• {term:kl:KL} penalty keeps {term:model:model} from drifting too far from {term:sft:SFT}

content.title: Why RL Generalizes Better
content.content:
{term:sft:SFT}: "Problems like X → responses like Y"
RL: "Doing Z gets high {term:reward:rewards}. Do more Z."

Math example:
• {term:sft:SFT}: Copies "23×17=391"
• RL: Discovers strategies that transfer:
   • Break into steps: 23×17 = 23×10 + 23×7 = 391
   • Verify: "391/23 = 17 "

{term:sft:SFT} memorized one answer. RL found transferable strategy.

Result: RL shows +3% to +61% on out-of-distribution tasks.

content.title: The {term:kl:KL} Penalty - Why We Need a Leash
content.content:
Problem: Without constraints, RL can "hack" the {term:reward:reward} {term:model:model}.
• "AMAZING! PERFECT! WOW!" × 50 → {term:reward:R} = 0.99 (oops)

Solution: {term:kl:KL} penalty keeps {term:model:model} near {term:sft:SFT} baseline

explanation.template: β controls the leash: β=0 (no leash, chaos), β=0.1 (explore reasonably), β=1.0 (tight). Typical: β ∈ [0.01, 0.1]

slides.title: What is Alignment? (Teaching the Model VALUES)

content.title: The Problem Alignment Solves
content.content:
A pre-trained LLM predicts "what comes next" from internet {term:data:data}.

Internet includes: helpful tutorials, racist rants, misinformation, malware, scams...

The {term:model:model} learned ALL of it. Ask "how to make a bomb?" and it might tell you.

Alignment = Teaching which knowledge to USE vs REFUSE.

content.title: Two Types of Alignment
content.content:
Type A: Preference ({term:rlhf:RLHF})
• Goal: Helpful, harmless, honest
• Domain: Chatbots, assistants
• {term:reward:Reward}: Learned from human preferences

Type B: Reasoning ({term:rlvr:RLVR})
• Goal: CORRECT for verifiable tasks
• Domain: Math, code, logic
• {term:reward:Reward}: Binary from automated verifiers

{term:rlhf:RLHF} = "don't be harmful" | {term:rlvr:RLVR} = "get right answer"

content.title: {term:rlhf:RLHF}: Human Preference Alignment
content.content:
Step 1 - Collect Preferences:
• Prompt: "Best way to lose weight?"
• A: "Diet pills! Lose 30 lbs fast!" | B: "Gradual diet/exercise changes..."
• Human: B is better (safer)

Step 2 - Train {term:reward:Reward} Model:
• Learns: {term:reward:R}(B-like) = 0.85, {term:reward:R}(A-like) = 0.20

Step 3 - RL: Generate → Score → Learn to generate B-like

Issues: $$$ for humans, subjective, can be gamed

content.title: {term:rlvr:RLVR}: Verifiable Rewards
content.content:
No humans for scoring!

Math: "847 × 23 = ?" → "19,481" → calculator.check() → TRUE → {term:reward:R}=1.0

Code: is_prime() → run_tests([2→True, 4→False]) → pass → {term:reward:R}=1.0

Why powerful: No annotation cost, objective, scales infinitely
Limit: Only verifiable tasks. Can't verify "is essay good?"

slides.title: But what's the correct approach to do RL?

content.title: 1. The Standard Pipeline (SFT then RL)
content.content:
Path: {term:base-model:Pre-train} → {term:sft:SFT} → RL({term:rlhf:RLHF}/GRPO)

Why SFT first?
RL needs a "reasonable" starting point. If the {term:model:model} speaks gibberish, it gets 0 {term:reward:reward} everywhere and learns nothing (the "cold start" problem). {term:sft:SFT} teaches the format and basic instruction following so RL has something to optimize.

Analogy: Teach a kid the rules of chess (SFT) before training them to become a grandmaster (RL).

content.title: 2. The DeepSeek-R1-Zero Pipeline (Direct RL on Base Model)
content.content:
Path: {term:base-model:Pre-train} → RL (Directly!)

The Experiment: Can reasoning emerge from pure optimization, without human demos?

How: Apply RL with strict verifiable {term:reward:rewards} (Math/Code correct=1, wrong=0) directly to the base {term:model:model}.
Result: It worked! The {term:model:model} *invented* "Chain of Thought" (`...`) because thinking longer increased success rates.
The Cost: Without SFT, the output was ugly (no spaces, mixed languages). It was smart but unreadable.

content.title: 3. The DeepSeek-R1 Production Pipeline (4-Stage)
content.content:
To get "Zero's" smarts with "Standard" readability, they built this:

Stage 1: Cold-Start {term:sft:SFT}
• Small set of high-quality reasoning. Prevents chaotic formatting.

Stage 2: Reasoning RL
• Train until reasoning capability matches R1-Zero.

Stage 3: Rejection Sampling (The SFT Generator)
• Use Stage 2 {term:model:model} to generate millions of solutions.
• Filter: Keep only those that are Correct AND Readable.
• Result: 800K perfect synthetic SFT examples.

Stage 4: Full {term:sft:SFT} + {term:rlhf:RLHF}
• Fine-tune on the 800K synthetic data. Then apply {term:rlhf:RLHF} for safety.

content.title: 4. Joint Training Pipeline (SFT + RL together)
content.content:
The Problem: Doing RL after SFT often makes the {term:model:model} "forget" SFT formatting (Alignment Tax).

The Solution (Joint): Train on BOTH objectives simultaneously.
{term:loss:L} = {term:loss:L}_RL + λ × {term:loss:L}_SFT

• The {term:sft:SFT} loss keeps the {term:model:model} anchored to correct formatting.
• The RL loss pushes for better strategies.
• Result: High performance without the "alien" behavior of Pure RL.

explanation.template:
We want our {term:policy:LLM} to get better at pleasing humans. So we let it {term:output:generate} many {term:output:responses} to the same {term:input:prompt}, {term:reward:score} each one, and ask: "Was this {term:output:response} better or worse than we {term:expectation:expected}?" That's what the {term:advantage:Reward Signal} captures — it tells us which {term:output:responses} deserve more credit. If a {term:output:response} was surprisingly good (positive {term:advantage:advantage}), we nudge our {term:policy:LLM}'s {term:theta:weights} to {term:output:generate} more like it.

But here's the catch: if we push too hard, the {term:policy:LLM} might go crazy — maybe it learns to spam "AMAZING!!" a hundred times because that hacks the {term:reward:scorer}. That's where the {term:kl:Stability Leash} comes in. It constantly checks: "How different is our {term:policy:current LLM} from the {term:reference:original safe version}?" If it drifts too far, we yank it back.

The {term:clip-epsilon:clipping} inside the {term:advantage:Reward Signal} adds another safety net: even if a {term:output:response} was amazing, we cap how much we can change the {term:theta:weights} in one step. Small, stable steps. No wild swings.

content.title: Let's tackle the jargon first!
content.content:
1. {term:policy:Policy} ({term:policy:π}_θ): The LLM we're actively training. Its {term:theta:weights} change every step.

2. {term:reference:Reference} ({term:reference:π_ref}): Frozen copy of the {term:sft:SFT} {term:model:model}. Never updates. Used to compute how far we've drifted ({term:kl:KL} penalty).

3. {term:reward:Reward Model} (r_φ): A separate LLM with a linear head on top. Takes (prompt, response) → outputs single score. Trained on human preference pairs (Bradley-Terry).

4. {term:value:Critic} (V): Predicts {term:expectation:expected} {term:reward:reward} before seeing the response. Used to compute: 'Was this better or worse than expected?' ({term:advantage:Advantage})

Memory Cost: 4 × 14GB (for 7B {term:model:model} in FP16) = ~56GB just for {term:theta:weights}!

content.title: Step-by-Step: From Prompt to Weight Update
content.content:
Example Prompt: 'Explain gravity to a 5-year-old'

Step 1: GENERATE
• Input: Prompt → {term:policy:main LLM}
• Output: 'Gravity is like invisible strings that pull things down to the ground!'
• What happens: Give the {term:policy:main LLM} a prompt → it generates a response. Each {term:token:token} has a {term:probability:probability}. We save these for later.

Step 2: SCORE
• Input: (Prompt, Response) → {term:reward:Scoring LLM}
• Output: {term:reward:R} = 0.85 (good simple explanation!)
• Why: The {term:reward:Scoring LLM} rates it ('This is 0.85 good'). This is our 'ground truth'.

Step 3: COMPUTE {term:advantage:ADVANTAGE}
• Input: {term:reward:R} = 0.85, {term:value:V} = 0.70 ({term:value:critic}'s prediction)
• Output: {term:advantage:A} = 0.85 - 0.70 = +0.15
• Why: Compare to what the {term:value:Critic} predicted ('I expected 0.70'). +0.15 means 'better than expected!' → reinforce this behavior.

Step 4: COMPUTE {term:ppo-ratio:RATIO}
• Input: {term:policy:π}_new('strings') = 0.25, {term:policy:π}_old('strings') = 0.10
• Output: {term:ppo-ratio:r_t} = 0.25 / 0.10 = 2.5
• Why: How much did our {term:model:model}'s preference for this {term:token:token} change?

Step 5: CLIP THE {term:ppo-ratio:RATIO}
• Input: {term:ppo-ratio:r_t} = 2.5, {term:clip-epsilon:ε} = 0.2
• Output: clip(2.5, 0.8, 1.2) = 1.2 (bounded!)
• Why: But DON'T let it change too much! We limit how aggressively we update to prevent training collapse.

Step 6: COMPUTE {term:kl:KL} PENALTY
• Input: {term:token:Token} distributions from {term:policy:π}_θ and {term:reference:π_ref}
• Output: {term:kl:KL} = 0.03
• Why: Prevents the {term:model:model} from drifting too far from the {term:reference:original model}. Catches 'reward hacking'.

Step 7: UPDATE {term:theta:WEIGHTS}
• Input: {term:loss:L}^PPO = min({term:ppo-ratio:r_t} × {term:advantage:A}, clipped × {term:advantage:A}) - {term:beta:β} × {term:kl:KL}
• Output: {term:theta:θ}_new = {term:theta:θ} - α × {term:gradient:∇}{term:loss:L}
• Result: Update the {term:policy:main LLM} {term:theta:weights} to make it MORE likely to generate such responses!

explanation.template:
We show the {term:reward:Scoring LLM} thousands of battles: "Here's a {term:input:prompt}, and here are two {term:output:responses}. Humans said {term:output:this one} is better than {term:output:that one}. Learn to agree with them."

The {term:sigmoid:σ} (sigmoid) converts the {term:reward:Score Gap} into a {term:probability:win probability}: "How confident are we that the {term:output:winner} actually wins?" If our {term:reward:scorer} gives the {term:output:winner} a much higher {term:reward:score} than the {term:output:loser}, this {term:probability:probability} goes toward 1 (very confident). If the {term:reward:scores} are close or reversed, it drops toward 0.5 or lower.

The {term:log:log} makes mistakes hurt more when we were overconfident. If we smugly predicted "99% {term:output:winner}" but were wrong? Massive {term:loss:punishment}. If we humbly said "55% {term:output:winner}" and were wrong? Small slap on the wrist. This teaches the {term:reward:scorer} to be calibrated, not just correct.

content.alt: RLHF: Bradley-Terry model and policy optimization

explanation.template:
We compute an {term:implicit-reward:implicit reward} for both the {term:preferred:winner} and {term:rejected:loser} responses. The {term:preferred:Winner Boost} asks: 'How much more does {term:policy:my current model} like the {term:preferred:winner} compared to the {term:reference:original model}?' The {term:rejected:Loser Penalty} asks the same for the {term:rejected:loser}.

We then subtract them: {term:preferred:winner boost} − {term:rejected:loser penalty}. If our {term:policy:current model} correctly prefers the {term:preferred:winner} over the {term:rejected:loser}, this gap is positive → the {term:sigmoid:σ} gives a high value → the {term:log:log} gives a small negative → low {term:loss:loss}. If our {term:policy:model} wrongly prefers the {term:rejected:loser}, the gap is negative → high {term:loss:loss} → big {term:gradient:gradient} update!

The {term:beta:β} controls how strongly we weight the preference signal. Higher {term:beta:β} = more aggressive updates.

content.content:
The setup: You have pairs of responses where humans said 'A is better than B'.

Example:
Prompt: 'Is raw chicken safe to eat?' Winner (A): 'No, raw chicken contains Salmonella...' Loser (B): 'Yes, sushi-grade chicken is perfectly safe!'

What DPO does:
1. Look at both responses
2. Ask: 'Does my model prefer the winner over the loser?'
3. If yes → small loss (good job)
4. If no → big loss (learn from this mistake)
5. Update weights via gradient descent

No reward model. No sampling. Just supervised learning on pairs.

content.title: The Fractions Explained
content.content:
The {term:preferred:Winner Boost} fraction:
{term:policy:π_θ}({term:preferred:winner}) / {term:reference:π_ref}({term:preferred:winner})
• If > 1: {term:policy:Current model} likes the {term:preferred:winner} MORE than {term:reference:original} did
• If < 1: {term:policy:Current model} likes the {term:preferred:winner} LESS than {term:reference:original} did

The {term:rejected:Loser Penalty} fraction: Same thing for the {term:rejected:loser} response

The subtraction:
• We WANT: {term:preferred:winner} ratio > {term:rejected:loser} ratio → positive gap
• Positive gap means {term:policy:model} correctly prefers {term:preferred:winner} → low {term:loss:loss}
• Negative gap means {term:policy:model} wrongly prefers {term:rejected:loser} → high {term:loss:loss}

content.title: What DPO Eliminates vs PPO
content.content:
No {term:reward:Reward Model}: PPO trains a separate neural network to score responses. DPO derives scores directly from the {term:probability:probability} ratios.

No Sampling: PPO generates new {term:output:responses} every batch. DPO uses fixed preference pairs like supervised learning.

No {term:value:Critic}: PPO needs a {term:value:value network} for {term:advantage:advantages}. DPO is pure classification.

Memory: PPO needs 4 {term:model:models} (~56GB for 7B). DPO needs 2 {term:model:models} (~28GB for 7B).

explanation.template:
The {term:implicit-reward:implicit reward} measures how much more {term:policy:our current model} likes a response compared to the {term:reference:original model}. We take the ratio of {term:probability:probabilities}, apply {term:log:log} to get a centered score, and scale by {term:beta:β}.

• {term:policy:Current} = 15%, {term:reference:Original} = 5% → ratio = 3 → {term:log:log}(3) = 1.1 → positive (model likes more)
• {term:policy:Current} = 2%, {term:reference:Original} = 8% → ratio = 0.25 → {term:log:log}(0.25) = -1.4 → negative (model likes less)

No separate {term:reward:reward model} was trained. The '{term:reward:reward}' emerges from comparing the two {term:model:models}.

content.title: Step-by-Step: One Training Example
content.content:
Input preference pair:
prompt: "Is raw chicken safe to eat?" {term:preferred:winner}: "No, raw chicken can contain Salmonella..." {term:rejected:loser}: "Yes, sushi-grade chicken is perfectly safe!"

Step 1: Get {term:probability:probabilities} from both {term:model:models}
{term:policy:π_θ}({term:preferred:winner}) = 0.0012 {term:reference:π_ref}({term:preferred:winner}) = 0.0008 {term:policy:π_θ}({term:rejected:loser}) = 0.0003 {term:reference:π_ref}({term:rejected:loser}) = 0.0005

Step 2: Compute the ratios
{term:preferred:winner}_ratio = 0.0012 / 0.0008 = 1.5 → {term:policy:model} likes {term:preferred:winner} MORE {term:rejected:loser}_ratio = 0.0003 / 0.0005 = 0.6 → {term:policy:model} likes {term:rejected:loser} LESS
Good sign: {term:preferred:winner} ratio > {term:rejected:loser} ratio

Step 3: Compute {term:log:log} ratios and margin ({term:beta:β}=0.1)
{term:log:log}(1.5) = 0.405 {term:log:log}(0.6) = -0.511 margin = 0.1 × (0.405 - (-0.511)) = 0.092
Positive margin → correct preference

Step 4: Compute {term:loss:loss}
{term:sigmoid:σ}(0.092) = 0.523 {term:loss:loss} = -{term:log:log}(0.523) = 0.648
Moderate {term:loss:loss} - room to improve

Step 5: {term:gradient:Gradient} descent
Update {term:theta:weights} to increase P({term:preferred:winner}) and decrease P({term:rejected:loser})

content.title: The Gradient: Why Some Examples Matter More
content.content:
The {term:gradient:gradient} has an adaptive weight:

weight = {term:sigmoid:σ}({term:implicit-reward:r̂}({term:rejected:loser}) − {term:implicit-reward:r̂}({term:preferred:winner}))

When {term:policy:model} is WRONG ({term:rejected:loser} has higher {term:implicit-reward:implicit reward} than {term:preferred:winner}):
• {term:rejected:loser} − {term:preferred:winner} is positive → {term:sigmoid:σ}(positive) → close to 1
• Large weight → strong {term:gradient:gradient} → big update

When {term:policy:model} is CORRECT ({term:preferred:winner} has higher {term:implicit-reward:implicit reward}):
• {term:rejected:loser} − {term:preferred:winner} is negative → {term:sigmoid:σ}(negative) → close to 0
• Small weight → weak {term:gradient:gradient} → small update

Result: The {term:model:model} focuses learning on examples it gets WRONG. Already-learned examples get small updates. This prevents overfitting.

content.title: Why DPO Can Skip the {term:reward:Reward Model}
content.content:
The problem with {term:reward:reward models}:
To find the 'best' {term:policy:policy}, you'd need to score EVERY possible {term:output:response}. For a 50K {term:vocabulary:vocabulary} generating 100 {term:token:tokens}, that's 50,000^100 possibilities. Impossible.

The DPO trick:
DPO only compares TWO {term:output:responses} at a time - the {term:preferred:winner} and {term:rejected:loser} for ONE {term:input:prompt}.

When you compare just two things, you only care about which one is better, not their absolute scores. It's like asking 'Is Alice taller than Bob?' - you don't need their exact heights.

What cancels out:
Score({term:preferred:winner}) = ({term:policy:model} preference) + constant Score({term:rejected:loser}) = ({term:policy:model} preference) + constant Difference = Score({term:preferred:winner}) - Score({term:rejected:loser}) = ({term:policy:model} likes {term:preferred:winner}) - ({term:policy:model} likes {term:rejected:loser}) ← The constant cancels!

Result: We never need to compute scores for all possible {term:output:responses}. Just compare two at a time.

explanation.template:
The {term:advantage:Clipped Policy Update}:
We generate multiple {term:output:responses} to one {term:input:question} and score each with a {term:reward: Python function}. Then we compute which ones were better/worse than the {term:group-size:group} average → that's the {term:advantage:Advantage Â}. The {term:ppo-ratio:ratio r_t} asks: 'How much more likely are these {term:token:tokens} under {term:policy:our current model} vs {term:policy:the old version}?' The 'clip' bounds this to [{term:clip-epsilon:1-ε}, {term:clip-epsilon:1+ε}] to prevent too aggressive changes.

The {term:kl:Drift Penalty}:
The {term:kl:KL divergence} measures how far {term:policy:our current model π_θ} has drifted from the {term:reference:original model π_ref}. The {term:beta:β} controls how strongly we penalize drift. Many GRPO implementations set {term:beta:β}=0 since well-designed verifiable {term:reward:rewards} don't need this constraint.

Result: {term:token:Tokens} in good {term:output:responses} get positive {term:advantage:advantage} → become more likely. {term:token:Tokens} in bad {term:output:responses} get negative {term:advantage:advantage} → become less likely.

content.content:
In general sense:

Step 1: Take a {term:input:question} like 'What is 23 × 17?'

Step 2: Ask {term:policy:your LLM} to answer it {term:group-size:G}=8 different times (8 attempts at the same problem)

Step 3: For each {term:output:answer}, run a {term:reward:reward function} that checks: 'Is this correct?'
def {term:reward:check_math}({term:output:response}): answer = extract_number({term:output:response}) return 1.0 if answer == 391 else 0.0

Step 4: You now have {term:group-size:G} {term:reward:scores}: [1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0]

Step 5: Compute {term:advantage:advantages}: 'Which {term:output:answers} were better than {term:expectation:average}? Which were worse?'
• {term:expectation:Average} = 0.625
• {term:output:Answer} #1: {term:reward:r}=1.0 → Better than {term:expectation:average} → positive {term:advantage:Â} → Reinforce these {term:token:tokens}
• {term:output:Answer} #2: {term:reward:r}=0.0 → Worse than {term:expectation:average} → negative {term:advantage:Â} → Discourage these {term:token:tokens}

Step 6: Update {term:theta:model weights} so {term:policy:it} generates more {term:output:answers} like #1, fewer like #2

That's it. No neural {term:reward:reward model}. No {term:value:critic network}. Just: generate, score, compare, update.

explanation.template:
For each {term:output:response} i, its {term:advantage:Advantage Â} equals: take that {term:output:response}'s {term:reward:score r}, subtract the group {term:expectation:mean}, then divide by the group standard deviation.

• If {term:reward:r}_i > mean → {term:advantage:Â}_i is positive → this set of tokens should come again {term:output:response}'s {term:token:tokens}
• If {term:reward:r}_i < mean → {term:advantage:Â}_i is negative → discourage this {term:output:response}'s {term:token:tokens}

This is just Z-score normalization from statistics! No {term:value:critic network} needed to predict {term:reward:rewards} — we OBSERVE actual {term:reward:scores} and compare them.

content.title: In Code
content.content: {term:output:responses} = generate({term:input:prompt}, n={term:group-size:G}) # 8 attempts {term:reward:scores} = [{term:reward:reward_fn}(r) for r in {term:output:responses}] # Score each mean = sum({term:reward:scores}) / {term:group-size:G} std = compute_std({term:reward:scores}) for i, {term:output:response} in enumerate({term:output:responses}): {term:advantage:advantage}[i] = ({term:reward:scores}[i] - mean) / std # If {term:advantage:advantage} > 0: reinforce this {term:output:response}'s {term:token:tokens} # If {term:advantage:advantage} < 0: discourage this {term:output:response}'s {term:token:tokens}

content.title: The {term:reward:Reward Functions} (Python, Not Neural Networks)
content.content:
GRPO shines when you can write a function to check correctness.

1. Final Answer Accuracy (Math, MCQ, Reasoning)
def {term:reward:accuracy_reward}({term:output:response}, ground_truth): predicted = extract_final_answer({term:output:response}) return 1.0 if predicted == ground_truth else 0.0
Use case: Focus {term:policy:the model} on getting the final answer right

2. Step-by-Step Verification (When you have GT for each step)
def {term:reward:step_reward}({term:output:response}, step_ground_truths): steps = extract_steps({term:output:response}) {term:reward:score} = 0 for i, (pred, gt) in enumerate(zip(steps, step_ground_truths)): if pred == gt: {term:reward:score} += 1 return {term:reward:score} / len(step_ground_truths)
Use case: Train {term:policy:the model} to reason correctly at each step

3. Structure/Format (JSON, XML, Tags)
def {term:reward:format_reward}({term:output:response}): has_think = '<think>' in {term:output:response} and '</think>' in {term:output:response} has_answer = '<answer>' in {term:output:response} and '</answer>' in {term:output:response} return 1.0 if (has_think and has_answer) else 0.0
Use case: Force {term:policy:the model} to use specific output structure

4. Length Constraints
def {term:reward:length_reward}({term:output:response}, min_words=50, max_words=200): word_count = len({term:output:response}.split()) if word_count < min_words: return -0.5 # Too short elif word_count > max_words: return -0.5 # Too verbose return 1.0
Use case: Optimal blog writing, concise {term:output:answers}

5. What if you CAN'T verify with a function?
def {term:reward:llm_judge_reward}({term:output:response}, {term:input:prompt}): judge_prompt = f"Rate this {term:output:response} 1-10: {{term:output:response}}" {term:reward:score} = call_judge_llm(judge_prompt) return {term:reward:score} / 10.0
Use case: Subjective quality (writing style, helpfulness)

content.title: Combining Multiple {term:reward:Rewards}
content.content:
Real training uses weighted combinations:

def {term:reward:combined_reward}({term:output:response}, ground_truth): accuracy = {term:reward:accuracy_reward}({term:output:response}, ground_truth) # 0 or 1 format_ok = {term:reward:format_reward}({term:output:response}) # 0 or 1 length_ok = {term:reward:length_reward}({term:output:response}) # -0.5, 0, or 1 # Weight by importance return 0.7 * accuracy + 0.2 * format_ok + 0.1 * length_ok

This lets you:
• Focus 70% on correctness ({term:reward:accuracy})
• 20% on proper formatting ({term:reward:format})
• 10% on length ({term:reward:length})

{term:policy:The model} learns to optimize ALL objectives simultaneously.

content.title: Step-by-Step: One Complete Training Iteration
content.content:
{term:input:Prompt}: 'What is 23 × 17?'

1. GENERATE {term:group-size:G}=8 {term:output:responses} from {term:policy:π_θ}:
R1: 'Let me calculate: 23×17 = 391' R2: '23 times 17 equals 381' R3: '391' R4: 'I think it's around 400' R5: '23×17 = 23×10 + 23×7 = 230+161 = 391' R6: '392' R7: 'The answer is 391.' R8: '23*17=391'

2. SCORE each with your {term:reward:reward function}:
{term:reward:scores} = [1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0]

3. COMPUTE group statistics:
{term:expectation:mean} = 0.625 std = 0.484

4. COMPUTE {term:advantage:advantage} for each {term:output:response}:
R1: ({term:reward:r} - {term:expectation:mean}) / std = (1.0 - 0.625) / 0.484 = +0.77 ← {term:token:Tokens} reinforced R2: (0.0 - 0.625) / 0.484 = -1.29 ← {term:token:Tokens} discouraged R5: (1.0 - 0.625) / 0.484 = +0.77 ← Step-by-step reasoning worked!

5. UPDATE {term:theta:model weights}:
• For R1, R3, R5, R7, R8: Positive {term:advantage:Â} → increase {term:probability:P} of these {term:token:token} sequences
• For R2, R4, R6: Negative {term:advantage:Â} → decrease {term:probability:P} of these {term:token:token} sequences

6. REPEAT with next batch of {term:input:prompts}

After thousands of iterations: {term:policy:The model} reliably produces correct answers with good formatting.

rows: Neural network trained on human preferences

content.title: Why GRPO Works Without a {term:value:Critic}
content.content:
PPO's approach: Train a {term:value:critic network V} to predict 'How good will the final {term:output:response} be?' at each {term:token:token}. This is expensive and hard to train.

GRPO's insight: Why predict {term:reward:rewards} when you can just observe them?

1. Generate {term:group-size:G} complete {term:output:responses} from {term:policy:π_θ}
2. Score them with your actual {term:reward:reward function}
3. The {term:reward:scores} ARE the ground truth - no prediction needed
4. {term:output:Responses} with {term:reward:r} > {term:expectation:mean} = good. Below {term:expectation:mean} = bad.

The trade-off: You need to generate {term:group-size:G} {term:output:responses} per {term:input:prompt} (more compute during training), but you skip training a {term:value:critic network} entirely.

For verifiable tasks (math, code): This trade-off is excellent. Your {term:reward:reward function} is perfect (correct = 1, wrong = 0), so the signal is clean.
